data.title: Fixed drug eruption — viva
data.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Fixed drug eruption** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. What is a fixed drug eruption (FDE)?**
- Drug eruption that recurs at exactly the same site(s) each time the drug is taken, often adding new sites — usually 30 min to 8 h after re-exposure (first exposure: 1–2 weeks)

**Q2. Common culprit drugs (India).**
- Cotrimoxazole and sulphonamides, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin), NSAIDs (paracetamol, ibuprofen, oxicams, metamizole), tetracyclines, metronidazole/tinidazole, fluconazole, dapsone, barbiturates, phenolphthalein laxatives, carbamazepine
- Food and colours can cause it (fixed food eruption)

**Q3. Describe the lesion.**
- One or a few sharply demarcated round/oval dusky red to violaceous plaques, may blister centrally; burning/itching
- Heals with persistent slate-grey/brown hyperpigmentation (more marked in dark skin) which darkens and enlarges with each episode
- Sites: lips, genitals (glans penis — commonest site in men), hands, feet, face, oral mucosa
- Variants: generalised bullous FDE (GBFDE — mimics SJS/TEN, elderly, can be fatal), non-pigmenting FDE (pseudoephedrine), linear, eczematous, urticarial, wandering

**Q4. Pathogenesis — why does it recur at the same site?**
- Intra-epidermal resident memory CD8+ T cells (effector memory) persist at the healed site; on re-exposure they release IFN-γ, granzyme, perforin → keratinocyte death; regulatory T cells limit spread
- Explains the 'fixed' nature and rapid onset

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Interface dermatitis with many necrotic keratinocytes, mixed infiltrate including eosinophils and neutrophils, deep and superficial perivascular infiltrate, prominent pigment incontinence (melanophages) in dermis even in active lesions

**Q6. How do you confirm the culprit drug?**
- Detailed drug history and timeline; drug causality assessment (Naranjo scale, WHO-UMC)
- Patch test on the previously affected site (lesional patch test) — positive in ~40%; safe
- Oral provocation test with small dose under supervision (not for GBFDE); avoid if severe

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Genital: herpes simplex (recurrent vesicles, Tzanck/PCR), syphilitic chancre, Behçet's, traumatic ulcer
- Skin: EM (targets, acral), bullous insect bite, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, lichen planus pigmentosus, ashy dermatosis, mastocytoma, morphoea (early)
- GBFDE vs SJS/TEN: GBFDE has larger well-demarcated patches with intervening normal skin, less mucosal involvement, rapid onset, past history of similar episodes, better prognosis

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Identify and stop the drug; give the patient a written list of culprit and cross-reacting drugs (drug card)
- Topical potent steroid for non-erosive lesions; antiseptic/wet dressings for erosions; antihistamines
- GBFDE: manage like SJS/TEN in a burn-unit setting (cyclosporine/supportive)
- Pigmentation fades slowly; avoid re-exposure

**Q9. Why is cross-reactivity relevant?**
- Structurally related drugs (e.g. among fluoroquinolones, oxicam NSAIDs) may trigger the same lesions — test or avoid the whole class

**Q10. Generalised bullous FDE (GBFDE) in detail.**
- Multiple large dusky patches with blisters involving >10% BSA, few mucosal sites, elderly with comorbidities; mortality ~20% (similar to SJS/TEN); history of previous FDE at same sites; manage in burns unit, cyclosporine, avoid culprit

**Q11. Non-pigmenting FDE — features.**
- Large symmetrical erythematous plaques without residual pigmentation, often on hips, limbs; classically pseudoephedrine; also NSAIDs, piroxicam

**Q12. Oral provocation test — protocol and contraindications.**
- Start with 1/10–1/4 therapeutic dose under observation, increase stepwise; reaction within 30 min–8 h confirms; contraindicated in GBFDE, extensive mucosal involvement, pregnancy; informed consent

**Q13. Fixed food eruption — examples.**
- Cashew, peanut, lentils, strawberries, tonic water (quinine), food colours (tartrazine), aspartame; diagnosis by elimination and challenge

**Q14. Classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions by Gell–Coombs (revised).**
- Type I (IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Type II (cytotoxic antibody): drug-induced pemphigus, immune thrombocytopenic purpura
- Type III (immune complex): serum sickness, vasculitis
- Type IV T-cell: IVa (Th1 — contact dermatitis), IVb (Th2/ eosinophils — DRESS, MPE), IVc (cytotoxic — SJS/TEN, FDE, MPE), IVd (neutrophilic — AGEP)
- Non-immune: pseudo-allergy (MRGPRX2), phototoxic, pigmentation, overdose/ side effects

**Q15. Why does FDE heal with pigmentation more in Indians?**
- Basal keratinocyte damage leads to pigment incontinence — melanophages in dermis; darker skin with more melanin gives more prominent and prolonged slate-grey pigmentation

## Quick spotter facts
- Recurrent dusky plaque on glans at same site after drug — FDE
- Heals with slate-grey pigmentation
- Lesional patch test

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous adverse drug reactions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
